passage: Rain ended the sports period early, so Seema Miss let class five talk cricket in the school hall. Jomon was on his feet at once. "Number 7 is the best batter in the world. Remember his hundred against the Lions? And the sixty in the final?" Seema Miss asked, "What about the last four matches?" Jomon waved a hand. "The first one was the umpire's fault. Then the pitch was wet. Then the sun was in his eyes." A classmate held up the newspaper score card: 3, 0, 11, 5. Jomon folded his arms and shook his head. "That's just bad luck. Real fans know he's the best." A few children giggled, and he glared at them.

qa.q: What did the classmate hold up during the cricket talk?
qa.a: The classmate held up the newspaper score card showing 3, 0, 11 and 5.

qa.q: Why does it feel reasonable to Jomon to blame the umpire, the wet pitch and the sun?
qa.a: Jomon remembers the hundred and the sixty clearly, so the low scores feel like strange accidents rather than real evidence. Admitting them would feel like letting his hero down.

qa.q: What small step could help Jomon see the whole picture?
qa.a: He could write down every score from the season, good and bad, and look at them together before deciding who is best. Seema Miss could ask him to work out the average, which counts every match the same.

qa.q: How might the classmate with the score card see Jomon's reaction?
qa.a: The classmate may feel that no score will ever count as proof for Jomon, which could make talking cricket with him frustrating.

grounding: Shows a boy remembering only his favourite cricketer's big innings and explaining away the low scores as the umpire, the pitch or bad luck.

passage: I'm Nirmala, Gurpreet's didi, and my little brother, who is nine, has one hero: the team's left-arm fast bowler. Our bedroom wall is covered with his pictures. On Sunday the bowler gave away forty runs in four overs. Gurpreet switched off the TV and said the ball was wet, so it didn't count. Last month, when the same bowler took five wickets, Gurpreet replayed the highlights three times and cut the photo out of the paper. Yesterday Papa asked, "What about the match in Chennai?" Gurpreet said he didn't remember that one. I can't tell if he honestly forgot or just didn't want to. He only ever talks about the good days.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet say after the bowler gave away forty runs?
qa.a: Gurpreet switched off the TV and said the ball was wet, so it didn't count.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet be feeling when Papa brings up the match in Chennai?
qa.a: He may feel uncomfortable or defensive, because that match doesn't fit the picture of his hero. Saying he doesn't remember lets the happy story stay whole.

qa.q: How could Papa help Gurpreet look at the bowler more fairly without mocking him?
qa.a: Papa could sit with him and list every match of the season, the five-wicket day and the costly ones, and ask what the whole list says. Doing it as a shared game keeps Gurpreet from feeling attacked.

qa.q: How does Nirmala see her brother's habit?
qa.a: Nirmala notices that Gurpreet replays the good days and skips the bad ones, but she admits she can't tell whether he truly forgets or just prefers not to look.

grounding: Shows a boy keeping only his favourite bowler's good matches in memory and explaining away a bad one as a wet ball.

passage:
Monday: On the school bus, Gautam told Jaya that the captain had never failed in a big match. "Remember the final? Ninety-eight runs!"
Thursday: The captain was out for a duck in the semi-final. Gautam stared at the screen, then said loudly, "That was never out. The umpire needs glasses." When Jaya showed him the replay on her tablet, he said the camera angle was wrong.
Next Saturday: Jaya brought her cricket magazine, which had the captain's last ten scores in a table. Gautam read it slowly. Six were under twenty. "Magazines always pick the bad games," he muttered. But he kept looking at the table for a long time.

qa.q: How many of the captain's last ten scores were under twenty?
qa.a: Six of the captain's last ten scores in the magazine table were under twenty.

qa.q: Why did Gautam blame the camera angle when Jaya showed him the replay?
qa.a: His picture of the captain was built on the ninety-eight in the final, so the duck felt unfair rather than informative. Blaming the umpire and the camera protected that happy picture.

qa.q: What could Jaya try so that Gautam weighs the table instead of dismissing it?
qa.a: She could ask him to pick the scores himself, so the list isn't her evidence against him. Asking which result would make him change his view also helps him notice when he keeps only the good ones.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya when every bad score gets a new excuse?
qa.a: Jaya may feel that talking facts with Gautam goes nowhere, yet his long look at the table gives her a small hope that he is starting to notice.

grounding: Shows a boy over several days holding on to his captain's best innings and explaining away a duck and a poor run of scores.

passage: Lars had decided in the first week of term that Daniel was fake. Now, on the tram home through the grey Oslo drizzle, he scrolled back through the class group chat, hunting. Daniel had written "great goal, man" to the new boy: obviously sucking up. Daniel had put a heart under the teacher's post: trying too hard. Lars screenshotted both. He thumbed past Daniel's message from Tuesday offering everyone his notes for the chemistry test, and past the one wishing Lars luck at his handball match. Those didn't count; anyone could type nice words. His feed kept suggesting a video called "Signs someone is two-faced." He watched it twice, nodding along.

qa.q: What did Daniel offer everyone in his Tuesday message?
qa.a: Daniel offered everyone his notes for the chemistry test.

qa.q: Why does it feel reasonable to Lars to screenshot some messages and skip others?
qa.a: Lars already believes Daniel is fake, so he feels suspicious of every friendly message and quietly satisfied by any sign of effort he can call proof. Because he is so certain, collecting only those screenshots feels like fair evidence to him.

qa.q: What could Lars do to test his view more fairly?
qa.a: He could read the whole chat and sort every message from Daniel, including the notes offer and the good-luck wish, before judging. He could also ask what Daniel would have to do for Lars to see him as genuine.

qa.q: How might Daniel feel if he knew his kind messages were being read as fake?
qa.a: Daniel would probably feel hurt and confused, since even his offers of help were being turned into evidence against him.

grounding: Shows a teenager who has already judged a classmate as fake hunting the group chat for proof, skipping friendly messages while the feed serves matching videos.

passage: In the computer lab during free period, Preeti opened the class group chat instead of her project. Ever since Jagdish had topped the science quiz and then said "it was just luck," she had been sure he was fake-modest. She typed his name into the search bar and scrolled. "Happy birthday, Preeti!" Skip, everyone says that. "Anyone want to practise for the viva together?" Skip, just showing off. Then she found it: "lol I barely studied." She nudged her bench partner. "See? Liar. He studied all week." The partner shrugged. "He also sent me his diagrams yesterday." Preeti was already scrolling again, looking for the next one.

qa.q: What message did Preeti finally show her bench partner?
qa.a: She showed the message "lol I barely studied" from Jagdish.

qa.q: What does Preeti's skipping of the birthday wish and the practice offer suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: Preeti feels resentful that Jagdish called his quiz win luck, so kind messages seem like noise and only the boastful line feels meaningful. When she finds it she feels vindicated, though she is only looking for agreement.

qa.q: What went wrong in Preeti's search, and what could fix it?
qa.a: She searched to confirm her view rather than to check it. She could read every message of his, friendly and boastful, and ask whether the diagrams he shared fit her picture of him.

qa.q: How does the bench partner see Jagdish differently?
qa.a: The bench partner has received his diagrams and sees him as helpful, so the label of liar doesn't match that experience.

grounding: Shows a teenager searching a classmate's messages only for proof that he is fake and skipping the friendly ones.

passage:
Dear Mausi,
You asked about the new school. It's fine, except for Yogesh. Everyone thinks he's so nice, but I've figured him out. On Monday he told the teacher her saree was pretty. Total buttering. On Wednesday he laughed at Rhea's joke, which wasn't even funny, so obviously he's collecting friends. I keep a list in my notes now. Honestly, the internet agrees with me: every video I open lately is about fake friends, so it must be really common. Mummy says he carried my bag home when I twisted my ankle, but that was only because the sports teacher was watching. I'll send you the list if you want proof!
Love,
Swati

qa.q: According to Mummy, what did Yogesh do when Swati twisted an ankle?
qa.a: Mummy says Yogesh carried Swati's bag home after the ankle was twisted.

qa.q: Why does Swati feel so sure that the internet agrees?
qa.a: Swati feels confident because she keeps opening videos about fake friends, so more of them appear, and seeing them everywhere feels like proof that Yogesh fits the pattern.

qa.q: What would you advise Swati before sending the list?
qa.a: Swati could add a second column for the kind things Yogesh has done, like carrying the bag, and ask whether a fair judge would reach the same verdict. A break from those videos would also stop the feed echoing the idea back.

qa.q: How might Mausi read this email?
qa.a: Mausi may notice that every kind act gets an unkind explanation and wonder whether Swati is being fair, while still wanting to hear how the new school really feels.

grounding: Shows a teenager who has decided a classmate is fake reading each of his acts as proof, dismissing the kind ones, while the video feed keeps confirming the idea.

passage:
Tuesday, hostel room, 11 pm
Decided: no placements for me. I'm going for the design course abroad next year. Spent all evening "researching" and honestly I feel sorted. Read three blogs on why campus jobs kill creativity. Messaged Ankita, the senior who skipped placements and is now freelancing; she said it was the best decision of her life. Also found a thread where people called placement offers traps. The placement cell sent a mail with last year's numbers. Didn't open it, it's just propaganda. Didn't call Joseph bhaiya either, he'll only lecture me about loans. Anyway, I've done my homework. Feeling calm for the first time this week.
Francis

qa.q: Why did Francis not open the placement cell's mail?
qa.a: Francis called the mail with last year's numbers just propaganda and did not open it.

qa.q: Why does Francis feel calm and well researched?
qa.a: Francis has read several sources that all agree, so the decision feels checked and safe. What goes unnoticed is that everything likely to disagree, like the mail and Joseph bhaiya, was skipped.

qa.q: What could Francis add to make the research real?
qa.a: Francis could open the placement mail and call Joseph bhaiya on purpose, looking for the strongest case against skipping placements. If the plan still holds after that, the calm will be earned.

qa.q: How might Ankita's advice look from where Ankita stands?
qa.a: Ankita is one senior whose freelancing worked out, so her best decision reflects her own path; she may not know Francis's money situation or skills.

grounding: Shows a college student gathering only blogs, threads and a senior who agree with skipping placements, and ignoring the data and the relative who might disagree.

passage:
Vishal: ok final decision. skipping placements, going all in on the food-truck app 🚀
Usha: whoa. did you talk to anyone?
Vishal: tons. 3 seniors who dropped placements, all say it was the best move

Vishal: trust me, I've looked at this from every angle

qa.q: How many seniors did Vishal talk to?

qa.q: Why does Vishal feel the plan has been looked at from every angle?
qa.a: Vishal has read many articles and talked to several seniors, so it feels like a lot of research. Because all of it agrees with the decision already made, the missing side never feels like a gap.

qa.q: Which of Usha's questions could help Vishal most, and how could Vishal act on it?

qa.q: What is it like for Usha when every question gets brushed off?

grounding: Shows a college student who has decided to skip placements collecting only agreeing seniors and articles while calling it thorough research.

passage: On the evening bus from college back to her village near Hoshiarpur, Madhuri kept her phone close to her face. She had already told the placement coordinator she would sit out this year and prepare for the state services exam at home. Now she was collecting reasons. A coaching-centre poster at the bus stand read: "Selected students never waste time on private jobs." She photographed it. A cousin's forward about a topper who studied alone: saved. When Gurpreet, sitting beside her, said his elder brother had tried for three years and was now taking any job he could get, Madhuri nodded politely and looked out of the window. That night she told her mother she had checked every side.

qa.q: What did Madhuri photograph at the bus stand?
qa.a: She photographed a coaching-centre poster that said selected students never waste time on private jobs.

qa.q: Why does Madhuri feel she has checked every side?
qa.a: She has gathered a poster, a forward and her own plan, all pointing the same way, so it feels thorough. Gurpreet's story doesn't fit, so she lets it pass without weighing it.

qa.q: What could Madhuri try before telling her mother she had checked every side?
qa.a: She could ask Gurpreet's brother what those three years were like and find out how many people from her college cleared the exam. Hearing one disappointing story on purpose makes the choice stronger either way.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when Madhuri looks out of the window?
qa.a: Gurpreet may feel his brother's hard experience was brushed aside, and might hesitate to share honest warnings with her again.

grounding: Shows a college student who has already chosen to skip placements saving only the messages that agree and quietly ignoring a friend's warning.

passage: Okay, so you asked how I handled Payal's startup phase. I'm Indu, her roommate since first year, and for two months our room was one long pitch. Payal wanted to sell homemade pickles through a subscription app. Every time I raised a worry, like delivery costs, shelf life, or who pays monthly for pickles, she had an answer ready, and then she'd read me another comment from her post: "Genius!" "Take my money!" I argued every point and we both ended up sulking. What finally worked was one sentence, said gently over chai: "Payal, I've noticed you save every yes and delete every no." She went quiet. Next day she asked me to list the no's with her.

qa.q: What did Payal want to sell through a subscription app?
qa.a: Payal wanted to sell homemade pickles through a subscription app.

qa.q: Why did Payal keep reading out the encouraging comments?
qa.a: The praise made her feel the idea was already proven, and each comment made the worries seem small. Holding on to it also protected her excitement.

qa.q: Which approach worked better for Indu, and why?
qa.a: Arguing each point only left them both sulking, while gently naming the pattern let Payal see it for herself without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when her one gentle sentence finally got through to Payal?
qa.a: Indu probably felt relieved, after two months of arguing and sulking, that Payal went quiet and then asked her to list the no's together.

grounding: Shows a roommate watching a friend brush off every warning about a startup idea while quoting praise, and finding that naming the pattern kindly works better than debating.

passage: My name is Irawati, and I've shared a flat with Asif since second year. This month he has been planning a laundry pickup service for students, and I've watched the whole thing. When our other flatmate said most students just wash clothes in a bucket, Asif laughed it off. When a professor's email mentioned licences, he said, "That's for big companies." But when a junior commented "I'd use this!", he printed it and stuck it on the fridge. One evening I tried debating the numbers; he just got louder. On Sunday I said, "Can I tell you something I've noticed? You collect the yeses like stickers." He stared at the fridge for a long time. I don't know what he was thinking.

qa.q: What did Asif stick on the fridge?
qa.a: He printed a junior's comment, "I'd use this!", and stuck it on the fridge.

qa.q: What might Asif's long stare at the fridge suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest that the words landed and Asif felt unsettled, seeing the fridge as a wall of only yeses. Irawati admits not knowing for sure what he was thinking.

qa.q: What could Irawati do next to build on that Sunday talk?
qa.a: Irawati could offer to help Asif put the warnings, like the licences and the bucket washing, next to the praise and look at both together as a team rather than as a debate.

qa.q: How does the flatmate who mentioned bucket washing likely see Asif's reaction?
qa.a: The flatmate may feel brushed off, since a practical point got a laugh instead of a real answer.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing a friend dismissing every warning about a startup idea while keeping each encouraging comment, and naming the pattern gently after debate fails.

passage:
Monday, week one: At the canteen, Sahil explained his idea, an app for renting textbooks between juniors and seniors. Keerthana asked how he'd stop books coming back torn. "Details," he said, and showed her twenty thumbs-up on his poll.
Thursday, week two: A senior who had tried the same thing warned him about payment fights. Sahil told Keerthana the senior was "just bitter." She argued every point for an hour; he left annoyed.
Saturday, week four: On the hostel steps she tried something else. "I'm on your side. But I've noticed every warning becomes bitterness and every thumbs-up becomes proof." Sahil was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Okay. Who else tried this? I'll call them."

qa.q: What did Sahil show Keerthana when she asked about torn books?
qa.a: He showed her twenty thumbs-up on his poll.

qa.q: Why did Sahil call the senior "just bitter"?
qa.a: Sahil was excited and invested, so the warning felt like an attack on his dream. Calling the senior bitter let him keep the idea safe without weighing the payment problem.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's Saturday approach work better than the hour-long argument?
qa.a: Arguing point by point made Sahil defend himself, while naming the pattern kindly, and saying she was on his side, let him look at his own thinking without losing face.

qa.q: What might the senior who warned Sahil think on hearing about the Saturday talk?
qa.a: The senior would likely feel relieved that the warning finally counted for something, and might be glad to help when Sahil calls.

grounding: Shows a friend watching someone quote every encouraging vote and dismiss warnings about a startup, and shows that gently naming the pattern works better than arguing each point.

passage:
Hi Mukund,
Work's good, mostly. The team hired Chandrika two weeks ago and honestly I knew in her first meeting she wasn't sharp. She took ten seconds to answer a simple question. Since then it's been one thing after another: she spelt the client's name wrong in an email, and she asked where the printer was, twice. I've started keeping a note of it. Our manager keeps praising her client summary, but that was probably easy stuff. And yes, she stayed late to fix the dashboard bug, but anyone could have done that. I'll tell you more when we meet. I'm rarely wrong about people.
Sachin

qa.q: What did the manager keep praising?
qa.a: The manager kept praising Chandrika's client summary.

qa.q: Why does it feel sensible to Sachin to keep a note of Chandrika's slips?
qa.a: After the slow answer in the first meeting, Sachin already feels sure about her, so each slip seems like more proof and each success like an exception. To Sachin it feels like being observant.

qa.q: What could Sachin try to check that first impression?
qa.a: Sachin could keep a second list of her good work, like the client summary and the dashboard fix, and read both lists together before judging. Asking the manager what they valued in the summary would also help.

qa.q: How might Chandrika experience working next to someone who has already decided she is weak?
qa.a: She may sense that her effort, like staying late on the bug, is never noticed, which could make her anxious and less willing to ask simple questions.

grounding: Shows a young professional who judged a new colleague weak in her first meeting reading each small slip as proof while waving away her good work.

passage: You know, Varun, I'm the person on our team who spots weak links early. Pema's radar, everyone calls it. That new analyst, Hafsa? I had her figured out on day one. She asked what "the Q3 file" meant. Who asks that? Since then I notice everything: she sends reports at 6:02 instead of 6, she said sorry in one meeting three times. My lead says her data cleanup saved us a week. Fine, one good thing. But yesterday she missed a comma in a formula. See? That's the real Hafsa. People keep telling me to give her time. Why would I? I already know how this story ends.

qa.q: What does the lead say Hafsa's data cleanup did?
qa.a: The lead says her data cleanup saved the team a week.

qa.q: Why does Pema feel so sure about Hafsa after day one?
qa.a: Pema takes pride in spotting weak links early, so the first impression feels like skill rather than guesswork. Each small slip seems to confirm it, and the week saved gets filed as one good thing.

qa.q: What small step would help Pema judge Hafsa more fairly?
qa.a: Pema could list what Hafsa has actually delivered each week, including the cleanup, and ask whether a stranger reading that list would call her weak.

qa.q: How might Varun hear this story?
qa.a: Varun may notice that the evidence against Hafsa is tiny, like a comma and a two-minute delay, while the big result is waved away, and wonder how fair Pema is being.

grounding: Shows a young professional whose day-one impression of a new colleague turns each small slip into proof while her real results are dismissed.

passage: I sit between Arnab and the new designer, Meenal, so I've seen the whole thing. I'm Kalyani, by the way. On Meenal's first day she mixed up two client logos in a draft, and Arnab rolled his eyes and said, "Here we go." Since then he mentions every small thing in the morning meeting: a late reply, a font slightly off. Last Friday her poster for the festival campaign got the client's only compliment of the month. Arnab said the client was just being polite. I can't see inside his head; maybe he's stressed about his own work. But I notice he never says "good job" to her, and she's stopped showing him her drafts.

qa.q: What happened to Meenal's poster for the festival campaign?
qa.a: It got the client's only compliment of the month.

qa.q: What might Arnab be thinking when he calls the client's compliment just polite?
qa.a: He may feel irritated by Meenal and doubtful that anything good she does is real, because his day-one impression still feels true to him. Kalyani admits not knowing what is really in his head and wonders if he is stressed.

qa.q: How could Kalyani help without accusing Arnab?
qa.a: Kalyani could mention the compliment in the morning meeting alongside the small slips, or ask Arnab privately what Meenal would need to do to change his view.

qa.q: What is it like for Meenal to work next to Arnab?
qa.a: Meenal seems discouraged; she has stopped showing him drafts, which suggests she expects criticism whatever she does.

grounding: Shows a young professional who decided on day one that a new colleague was weak, now reading each slip as proof and dismissing her praised work.

passage: Lokesh, sit. Before you send that proposal, let me tell you about Vasudha. Twenty years ago she and I worked in the planning office of the water board. She was convinced a new pipeline route along the railway line was best, and she was usually right. But before the final meeting she did something odd. She came to my desk and said, "Shankar, you think my route is wrong. Give me your strongest reasons." Then she wrote on a slip: "If the soil report shows flooding, I drop this." She even read the rival engineer's full report twice, underlining what was good in it. The soil report came back clean, and her route was built. Nobody could say she hadn't listened.

qa.q: What did Vasudha write on the slip before the final meeting?
qa.a: She wrote, "If the soil report shows flooding, I drop this."

qa.q: Why did Vasudha ask Shankar for the strongest reasons against her route?
qa.a: She was confident but wanted her confidence to be earned; hearing the best objections from someone who disagreed felt safer than hearing only agreement.

qa.q: What could Lokesh borrow from Vasudha's method before sending the proposal?
qa.a: Lokesh could write down what result would prove the proposal wrong, then ask the most doubtful colleague for their best objections and read them carefully before deciding.

qa.q: How might the rival engineer have felt about Vasudha reading the report twice?
qa.a: The rival engineer would likely feel taken seriously, and could accept the final decision more easily because their work had been fairly weighed.

grounding: Shows a mature worker setting in advance what would make her drop her plan, asking a critic for the strongest objections and reading the opposing report before committing.

passage: The vendor wanted an answer by five, and the office internet had died at two. Sabina, the operations lead at a small logistics firm in Pune, was sure the cheaper warehouse in Chakan was the right choice. Still, with three hours left and no connection, she pulled out a notepad and wrote: "I switch if flood risk or road access is worse than I think." Then she walked to Karthik's cubicle, the one person who always disagreed with her. "Argue for the other warehouse. Your best version." He talked for twenty minutes about monsoon traffic on the Chakan road. She phoned a driver, who confirmed it. At 4:40 she signed for the costlier site, and thanked Karthik for being difficult.

qa.q: When did Sabina sign for the costlier site?
qa.a: She signed for the costlier site at 4:40.

qa.q: How can you tell that Sabina did not feel insulted by Karthik's disagreement?
qa.a: She sought him out because he always disagreed, asked for his best version, and thanked him afterwards, so his argument felt useful to her, not like an attack.

qa.q: Which step made Sabina's check work even without internet?
qa.a: Writing down in advance what would make her switch meant she knew exactly what to test, so one call to a driver could settle the road question before five.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Sabina thanks him for being difficult?
qa.a: Karthik would probably feel valued rather than resented, since his habit of disagreeing was treated as a help to the decision instead of a nuisance.

grounding: Shows a mature worker naming what would change her choice and asking her usual critic for the best opposing case, then letting that disagreement change her decision under time pressure.

passage: Parul had the slides ready: car-free Sunday mornings on the lake road in Kukatpally. She was sure. But on Friday evening, in the noisy municipal office, she turned to Ojas and asked, "Who will hate this most?" "The shop owners," he said. "Harish from their association wrote us a long letter." Parul printed all six pages and read them on the bus home, pen in hand. Some points were weak. One was not: the vegetable vendors' delivery vans came only on Sunday mornings. In her notebook she wrote, "If deliveries can't work, I rethink this." On Saturday she called Harish. "What would make this workable for you?" By Monday her plan had a delivery lane until nine.

qa.q: How many pages was the association's letter?
qa.a: The letter from Harish's association was six pages long.

qa.q: Why did Parul ask Ojas who would hate the plan most?
qa.a: Parul felt confident in the plan but was eager to find its weak spot before committing, so she treated the strongest opposition as useful information rather than a threat.

qa.q: What could other planners learn from Parul's weekend?
qa.a: They could read the opposing letter in full, call its writer with an open question, and let the one strong point reshape the plan instead of defending the original.

qa.q: How might Harish see the municipal office after Parul's call?
qa.a: Harish would probably feel heard, since the association's letter led to a real change, and may trust the office more in future talks.

grounding: Shows a mature worker seeking out the strongest critics, reading their full case and naming what would change her plan before committing to it.

passage: At the school's Saturday hobby club, Shankar from class seven had a shiny sheet of football stickers. "Fifty rupees," he said. Madhav gasped. That was nearly all his pocket money. "Forty?" "Forty-five." "Forty!" Shankar sighed dramatically and agreed. Madhav ran to the art table, grinning, and told his friend he'd saved ten whole rupees. The friend looked at the sheet. "The stationery shop outside the gate sells these for twenty." Madhav's smile wobbled. "But he said fifty first," he said slowly, as if that settled it. For the rest of the club hour he kept smoothing the sheet, not quite sure whether he had won or lost.

qa.q: What price did Shankar name first?
qa.a: Shankar first said fifty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Madhav feel he had saved ten rupees?
qa.a: Madhav treated fifty as the real price because it was the first number he heard, so paying forty felt like a win even though the shop charged twenty.

qa.q: What could Madhav try before the next swap or sale?
qa.a: He could first check what the stationery shop charges and decide his own top price before hearing any seller's number.

qa.q: How might Shankar see the bargain?
qa.a: Shankar probably feels pleased; starting at fifty made forty look generous, and he still earned double the shop price.

grounding: Shows a child treating a seller's first sticker price as the fair baseline, so a smaller but still high price feels like a big win.

passage: Every Sunday a man sets up a sticker cart outside our building, and last week I watched Devika, the eight-year-old from the second floor, bargain with him. I'm Manjula, Manju aunty to the children here, and I was buying coriander nearby. "Unicorn sheet, sixty rupees," he told her. Her eyebrows shot up. She offered forty; he said fifty-five; they settled at fifty. She skipped back past me, whispering, "I got ten off!" I didn't say anything. Your Joseph uncle
